prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Barack Obama reached out to Iran on Friday -- the start of the Iranian New Year -- in a video message offering "the promise of a new beginning" that is "grounded in mutual respect." Obama's message to Iran echoes his inaugural speech, where he said "we seek a new way forward." The message is a dramatic shift in tone from that of the Bush administration, which included Iran, along with North Korea and Iraq, in an "axis of evil." It also echoes Obama's inaugural speech, in which he said to the Muslim world, "we seek a new way forward, based on mutual interest and mutual respect." In Friday's video, Obama said: "The United States wants the Islamic Republic of Iran to take its rightful place in the community of nations. You have that right, but it comes with real responsibilities. And that place cannot be reached through terror or arms, but rather through peaceful actions that demonstrate the true greatness of the Iranian people and civilization." There was no immediate response from Tehran to Obama's message, but Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad said last month that his country would welcome talks with the United States "in a fair atmosphere with mutual respect." The United States, several European nations and Israel suspect that Tehran has been trying to acquire the capacity to build nuclear weapons, but Iran says its nuclear program is solely for peaceful purposes. Last month, the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security released a report saying that Iran has reached "nuclear weapons breakout capability" -- it has enough uranium to make a nuclear bomb. The report was based on an analysis of data from the International Atomic Energy Agency. However, an IAEA official who asked not to be named cautioned against drawing such dramatic conclusions from the data, saying Iran's stock of low-enriched uranium would have to be turned into highly enriched uranium to be weapons-grade material. That hasn't been done, the official said. The United States has had tortuous relations with Tehran since the Islamic revolution in 1979, but the Obama message speaks of "new beginnings" with the promise of a new year. "We have serious differences that have grown over time. My administration is now committed to diplomacy that addresses the full range of issues before us, and to pursuing constructive ties among the United States, Iran and the international community," the president said. "This process will not be advanced by threats. We seek, instead, engagement that is honest and grounded in mutual respect."

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Marking the beginning of the Iranian New Year on Friday, President Barack Obama addressed Iran through a video message that held out the prospect of a fresh start founded on reciprocal respect.

The outreach reflected language from Obama’s inauguration, when he told the Muslim world that the United States wanted to pursue a different path based on shared interests and respect. It represented a sharp change from the approach of the Bush administration, which had grouped Iran with Iraq and North Korea as part of an “axis of evil.”

In the video, Obama said Washington wanted the Islamic Republic of Iran to assume its proper role within the international community. He added that while Iran was entitled to such a position, it also had significant obligations. According to Obama, Iran could achieve that standing not through terrorism or weapons, but by taking peaceful steps that displayed the greatness of its people and civilization.

Tehran did not immediately react to the message. However, Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad had said the previous month that Iran would be open to discussions with the United States if they took place fairly and with mutual respect.

The United States, Israel and several European countries believe Tehran may be seeking the ability to produce nuclear weapons. Iran maintains that its nuclear activities are intended entirely for peaceful use.

A report issued the previous month by the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security concluded that Iran had attained a “nuclear weapons breakout capability,” meaning it possessed enough uranium to produce a nuclear bomb. The institute based its finding on data from the International Atomic Energy Agency.

An unnamed IAEA official, however, warned against making such far-reaching judgments from the information. The official noted that Iran’s supply of low-enriched uranium would first need to be converted into highly enriched, weapons-grade material—and said that conversion had not occurred.

Relations between Washington and Tehran have been deeply troubled since Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution. Nevertheless, Obama used the arrival of a new year to emphasize the possibility of a new beginning.

Acknowledging that major disagreements had accumulated over the years, Obama said his administration was committed to using diplomacy to address every issue between the parties and to developing productive relations among Iran, the United States and the wider international community. He stressed that threats would not move the process forward, and called instead for sincere engagement based on mutual respect.

President Barack Obama offered Iran a “new beginning” in a videotaped message marking Nowruz, the Persian New Year, signaling a significant change in tone from the administration of former President George W. Bush.

Addressing both the Iranian people and the leaders of the Islamic Republic, Obama said the United States wanted to overcome decades of mistrust through diplomacy. He called for engagement that was “honest and grounded in mutual respect,” while acknowledging that the two countries continued to have serious differences.

Obama said Iran could take its “rightful place in the community of nations,” but emphasized that this right came with responsibilities. He urged Tehran to pursue peaceful policies and suggested that international standing could not be achieved through terrorism, threats, or weapons, but through constructive engagement with other countries.

The message represented a sharp departure from the Bush administration’s approach. Bush had labeled Iran part of an “axis of evil” and generally sought to isolate Tehran over its nuclear program, support for militant groups, and hostility toward Israel. Obama’s appeal left open the possibility of renewed direct talks between the United States and Iran after nearly three decades without formal diplomatic relations.

At the time, Iran had not issued an immediate official response. Iranian leaders had previously said they wanted to see concrete changes in American policy rather than a shift in rhetoric alone, including a different approach to sanctions and U.S. involvement in the Middle East.

Concerns about Iran’s nuclear activities remained a central obstacle. International reports indicated that Tehran had accumulated a substantial amount of low-enriched uranium, prompting fears that the material could eventually be used to produce a nuclear weapon if it were enriched further. Iran maintained that its program was intended solely for peaceful purposes, including energy production.

Nuclear experts cautioned, however, that Iran’s existing uranium stockpile was not weapons-grade. Producing material suitable for a bomb would require additional enrichment and other technical steps, likely drawing international attention. Obama’s outreach therefore sought to create an opening for diplomacy while making clear that improved relations would depend on Iran’s willingness to address international concerns and act responsibly.

counterfactuals.output:
**Obama Extends Nowruz Message to Iran, Signaling Diplomatic Shift**

On March 20, 2009, President Barack Obama marked the start of Nowruz, the Iranian New Year, with a videotaped appeal for a “new beginning” in relations between the United States and Iran.

Addressing both the Iranian people and, unusually, the country’s leaders, Obama said Washington was committed to diplomacy grounded in “mutual respect.” His reference to the “Islamic Republic of Iran” was widely interpreted as recognition of Iran’s political system and a departure from previous U.S. efforts to isolate Tehran.

The conciliatory message contrasted sharply with President George W. Bush’s description of Iran, Iraq and North Korea as an “axis of evil” in 2002. While the Bush administration emphasized sanctions, pressure and the possibility of regime change, Obama said longstanding disputes should be resolved through engagement rather than threats. He nevertheless stressed that Iran’s place in the international community came with “real responsibilities.”

At the center of those disputes was Iran’s nuclear program. The United States and its allies feared that uranium enrichment and other activities could provide Iran with the capacity to build nuclear weapons. Tehran maintained that its program was intended solely for peaceful purposes, including energy production, and asserted its right to enrich uranium under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Iranian leaders responded cautiously. They welcomed changes in tone but said improved relations would require concrete shifts in U.S. policy and acknowledgment of past American actions against Iran. Obama’s Nowruz address did not resolve the nuclear confrontation, but it established direct engagement as a central feature of his administration’s approach and laid early groundwork for negotiations that eventually produced the 2015 nuclear agreement.

He spoke directly to both the Iranian people and Iran’s leaders, referred to the country by its official name—the “Islamic Republic of Iran”—and offered engagement based on “mutual respect.” Rather than emphasizing regime change, isolation, or military threats, he said Iran could take its “rightful place in the community of nations” through peaceful diplomacy.

# Obama Offers Iran ‘Promise of a New Beginning’

**WASHINGTON —** President Barack Obama has offered Iran “the promise of a new beginning,” using a videotaped message to call for direct engagement after three decades of hostility between Washington and Tehran.

In the message marking Nowruz, the Persian New Year, Obama addressed Iran’s people and leaders and said his administration was committed to diplomacy that “addresses the full range of issues before us.”

“The United States wants the Islamic Republic of Iran to take its rightful place in the community of nations,” Obama said. “You have that right — but it comes with real responsibilities.”

The outreach represented a sharp change in tone from the Bush administration, which included Iran in an “axis of evil” and sought to isolate Tehran over its nuclear program and support for militant groups.

Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad had previously said Tehran was prepared to consider talks with Washington if they were conducted on the basis of equality and mutual respect. But he also demanded concrete changes in U.S. policy, arguing that a different tone alone would not be enough to repair the relationship.

Iran’s leadership has repeatedly said its nuclear program is intended for civilian energy production. Western governments fear that the same technology used to enrich uranium for reactor fuel could eventually be used to produce weapons-grade material.

Recent data from the International Atomic Energy Agency showed that Iran had accumulated roughly a metric ton of low-enriched uranium and had installed several thousand centrifuges at its Natanz enrichment plant. Experts said the stockpile could, if further enriched and processed, potentially provide enough material for one nuclear weapon. That assessment did not mean Iran possessed a bomb or had decided to build one, and substantial additional technical work would be required.

Competing intelligence assessments have fueled disagreement over how close Iran may be to a nuclear capability. A 2007 U.S. National Intelligence Estimate concluded with high confidence that Iran had halted a coordinated nuclear-weapons program in 2003, while also warning that Tehran continued to develop enrichment technology that could give it the option of producing a weapon. Israeli officials and some outside analysts have offered more urgent assessments, arguing that Iran was approaching a point at which its nuclear infrastructure would be difficult to stop.

The IAEA has said it has not found proof that Iran diverted declared nuclear material to a weapons program. However, the agency has also said Tehran must provide greater cooperation and answers about past activities that could have military applications.

The dispute sits atop a long history of mistrust dating to Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution. Later that year, militants seized the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days, prompting Washington to break diplomatic relations.

Relations deteriorated further during the Iran-Iraq War, when the United States tilted toward Baghdad, and after a series of clashes in the Persian Gulf. In 1988, a U.S. Navy cruiser shot down Iran Air Flight 655, killing all 290 people aboard; Washington said the civilian aircraft had been mistaken for a hostile military plane.

Since then, the two countries have remained divided over U.S. sanctions, Iran’s support for Hezbollah and Palestinian militant groups, American military deployments in the region and Tehran’s nuclear activities. They have also found limited areas of overlapping interest, including opposition to the Taliban after the September 11 attacks and efforts to stabilize Iraq.

Obama’s message did not remove those disputes, nor did it offer immediate concessions. But by directly recognizing the Islamic Republic and emphasizing diplomacy, the president signaled that Washington was prepared to test whether decades of confrontation could give way to negotiations.

Whether that “new beginning” becomes substantive talks will depend on what each side is willing to do next.
